While often enshrined as a cinematic masterpiece, The Battle of Algiers reveals itself upon closer inspection to be a technically flawed work of state-sponsored propaganda that priorities political utility over artistic integrity. It is profoundly shallow in character observation and attempts to substitute the hollowness of the narrative with the heaviness of the topic (colonialism). As this film was commissioned by the Algerian government and produced by an FLN commander, the impact of other Algerian resistance movements are completely ignored and instead the film is to function as a seemingly authentic origin story propaganda. The film’s celebrated documentary aesthetic is revolutionary, but is undercut by multiple weak formal aspects. The lighting in particular is jarringly inconsistent, often featuring blindingly bright front-lighting in scenes where no logical light source exists. Even between cuts of the same scene, the front-lighting persists into the new perspective, resulting in continuity errors and shifting shadows that shatter the very immersion the film claims to cultivate. This is compounded by an uneven sound design that lack consistency in dynamic and integration. Furthermore, mechanical cuts stitch scenes together without transition or narrative juxtaposition. As a result, the film feel like a collection of in-cohesive fragments that lacks vision. As mentioned previously, the film disguises narrative depth by the weight of its topic rather than by the quality of its writing. Despite the film's attempt to imitate observational realism, characters are treated as hollow ideological devices rather than real humans beings. The much applauded non-professional actor, Brahim Hadjadj, performs an Ali la Pointe that is painfully one-dimensional and mechanical, providing no window into the character's psyche (to the point that it is difficult to even recognise him as the protagonist). Ironically, the "villainous" Colonel Mathieu is given more complexity and range, feeling slightly more like a real individual instead of just a hollow political vessel. The film’s most egregious flaw is its poorly executed mechanical emotional manipulation from its sound and visual language. Death and suffering of Algerians are accompanied with religious scores and manufactured tears to evoke sanctity and martyrdom. In contrast, the death of European innocents are treated with cold, percussive score and lack of emotional outburst (even from themselves) to trivialise the tragedy. Disregarding the intent, the ostentatious and un-serious execution results in theatricality that ends up losing emotional grounding. Ultimately, The Battle of Algiers is less a work of art and more a technical manual for insurgency. It fails the "show, don't tell" rule with its paradoxical, dry narration and expositions that explains the how of the conflict while speaking little on the historical why. Concerningly, the film also directly proclaims the effectiveness of terrorism as a mean to gain UN support as well as the potency of torture (despite many research indicate otherwise). In the film's final scene, the irony of shouting for independence in the language of the coloniser is perhaps the film's most profound and most honest observation about the lasting scars of imperialism, yet unsurprisingly this is a depth that clearly escapes the interest of the film.

my "remedial film school" project — catching up on the movies that most frequently turn up on greatest-of-all-time lists — has sometimes led to disappointments, but few have been as much of a struggle for me as this one. Admittedly it wasn't ideal viewing circumstances, pulling it up in fits and starts and consistently tuning out, such that it took me three or four sessions to make it through these two hours. I think it's just so unlike any film that I've seen before that I genuinely didn't know how to watch it, and the film was not in a hurry to teach me. Probably my biggest barrier is that it seems so disinterested in the humanity of everyone on screen — we don't follow hardly any characters consistently enough to get a sense of who they are as people, with the weird exception of Colonel Mathieu. Yes war dehumanizes everyone, but that doesn't mean the film needs to help the process along. Brahim Hadjadj plays Ali La Pointe as a sullen-faced silent type, which makes a certain amount of sense for his situation but makes him unengaging as the lead of a film. And the movie's weird dispassionate documentary-style tone means that I spent the whole time waiting for a moment of connection that never came. Time passes, people die, a series of events is shown, with little sense of causality or logic. But I suppose maybe frustrated restlessness is the desired effect after all?

Not a Cinematic Review The first time I saw this movie, I was amazed—I was a teenager then. But after reading more history and becoming anti-Marxist, I now see it as a very dangerous propaganda film. It glorifies leftist terrorism and the killing of innocents. Yes, the French government committed many atrocities against Algerians. They killed a lot of people and caused deep harm. But the outcome of the revolution led by the FLN is also tragic. When the socialists gained power, they became corrupt and destroyed the country. The Algerian people suffered just as much under their own rulers as they did under French colonialism. The only truly tragic element here is the people themselves. That said, this film is a cinematic masterpiece—and unfortunately, it inspired many terrorist groups around the world, including in Iran, Europe, and South America. It was even referenced in letters written by the Mujahedin, a socialist group in Iran before the revolution. In many ways, this film contributed to the ideology that caused decades of suffering for the Iranian people. So, while I admit it’s a powerful piece of cinema, as someone who has lived through revolution and seen the sadness of my people, I cannot love this movie. For me, it’s like being African American and watching The Birth of a Nation by D. W. Griffith—yes, it’s a cinematic masterpiece, but it's also deeply toxic in its message. To get to the point: as a film, it’s brilliant. The characters are layered, the villains are not pure evil—they have motives. The dialogue is tight and meaningful. The direction is phenomenal. The score by Ennio Morricone is haunting and unforgettable. My only critique from a film-lover’s perspective is that the main revolutionary character isn’t shown to be important enough. The villain spends the film hunting him down, and his death is presented as a major victory, but we never fully see why he matters. The story needed more to build his significance. Got so excited because the music in this is used in Inglorious Basterds [45] On the technical level in regards to the psychology, camera-work, and thematic weight the depictions in this hold, this is an astoundingly well-done film. It has quite literally been used by both resistance fighters and militaries to gain insight on how these movements can be ran, it was written by someone who was a member of the FLN (National Liberation Front), contained actors who had lived through the accounts detailed, and was shot on location where the events occurred. There are of course some historical inaccuracies, but by and large this is a frighteningly accurate depiction of this event, and furthermore it makes you feel like you're there. It's also important to note that both the French authorities and FLN did even worse things in real life. Specifically the French, as this really cannot capture the breadth of killings and abuse they inflicted on Algerians to get their way (also highlights how useless the UN is and has always been). And there's one specific scene in this movie that is absolutely the highlight for me where Colonel Mathieu claims they cannot be fascists or oppressors as many of them were part of the resistance movement fighting against the Nazis ( cough couch Israel cough couch ). But this line is just wonderful, and for me it beautifully illuminates the uncomfortable reality of brutality humans are capable of; if our worldview justifies it we can be just as capable of the evils we decry. And this also gets into the meat of the question this film is proposing: what is justified in my fight for freedom? We are definitely on the side of the FLN in terms of perspective, but the film never tries to state that they are the good guys (and while I think we can come to the conclusion that comparatively they were, they still weren't "good" guys). It inherently puts the question to us when we are watching them bomb places with civilians of "is this justified?" Personally I don't know, I would like to say they could've instead bombed military targets or done some other thing, but the reality very well may be that this was the only way to make effective change (and when you are trying to change the fact that you are being brutally oppressed by colonizers, that effective change is pretty darn important). It's also interesting as they are fully willing to shirk things such as Sharia Law to wage this war (such as the women disguising themselves as French women) when the aim is to be able to reinstate that law once they have gained their independence (a whole other decision that I believe would warrant a whole new version of FLN to fight against the oppression that that brings). In the end I think this is wonderful at making you have to weigh what is right in your own mind, and hopefully reassess your own beliefs. At the very least this movie shines a light bulb on an event (and an issue) that deserves to be known and talked about. France still hasn't issued an apology to Algeria (just how the U.S. hasn't to Vietnam about things as basic as the effects of agent orange, or Japan to China about Nanjing, nor Britain to India, etc. etc.) and while I do believe the status of the world is much better today, it takes a simple Google to see this is still occurring all over. And I believe the biggest part that makes it overwhelmingly depressing is that it is truly completely manufactured by humans to a degree that is mind-numbingly pointless. So why am I giving this such a review after going over all that which I have gleamed from the movie? Cause I didn't really enjoy watching it that much. While all of the above are true, I never found myself caring about the events of the story. Characters are barely fleshed out, and they jump from person to person so quickly it's impossible to truly get invested in any particular aspect. The bag drop off scene is easily the best as it gives enough room to breathe and let you ruminate with the emotions of the characters, but outside of this it is purely the analytics of what is being done and the loud declaration of why (which is of course always for a free Algeria or because France doesn't want to give up Algeria) with no real inspection into the characters and deeper motivations. It sets me at a removed distance from what is going on, and I unfortunately could care little less what would happen to everyone. Of course I am sad when innocents die, but that is because innocents died, not because of anything the film was doing to invest me. Freedom isn't free, but what cost are we willing to pay, and what does free even truly mean to us?

Apologies for bad grammar/typos I don’t like to read over my writing when I’m slightly annoyed at something. Ok so The Battle of Algiers sitting at a cozy 4.5 on this website and with almost every popular review raving about I am in an awkward position to have to go against the grain here and say the movie is just about fine. To be completely honest, I am a little bewildered by the outpouring of admiration for this thing. I actually struggle to put myself in the shoes of reviewers who write things like: “It takes a very real, overwhelming geopolitical situation and realizes it in the POV of human eyes and ears” (Josh Lewis - the most popular review) or “Brutal, unsparing, and as close the real thing as is possible on film” (Will Menaker - second most popular review). In my experience those comments are blatantly untrue. I’m going to attempt to explain the film as I saw it but I’m not sure it will translate to those who are so taken by these images. Firstly, I think it does a disservice to the Algerian people and to people in general who have the courage to really fight for their country and for their freedom. I think the characters drawn up by Pontecorvo are shells, at most their actions serve as thematic signifiers but even still that makes no difference in the experience of the film. I felt I might as well just be reading a wikipedia article. It feels almost impossible to imagine these people in any scenarios that are not the scenarios we see in the film, I sense no depth here and crucially therefore no humanity. The film opens with Ali La Pointe being discovered, a moment we know will spell his death, a complicated sacrifice that takes a child to the grave with him. How can a man come to be here? How does he feel in this moment? What is going through his head? We get nothing. Blank, emotionless, stoic expressions that I cannot possibly comprehend as real. A child is sitting here knowing he will face death equally as emotionless. If this is accurate (and I’m almost sure it is not) surely we should gain some insight into how a child has the qualities of stoicism and self sacrifice nurtured into him by his community. Surely there must be something here, some point being made by the filmmaker but no. Nothing is learned, nothing is revealed, I feel no more or less revolutionary than before I watched this. I have no more or less courage, I have no more or less passion, I have no more or less anything because this film does not serve you with anything that could possibly challenge the way you go through life. Ending sequences include masses of Algerians throwing themselves at French military who shoot them down and they fall rag-doll like and inspire no fear in the rest of the crowd. The really wild thing about this film is that the only people who seem to be shown with any depth are the French themselves. It’s weird. We see internal struggle there. Imperfection, racism, stupidity, complicity, ignorance, etc. but in the characters of the FLN barely any emotion is suggested. There is a long and poorly structured sequence of three women walking into various public places and leaving bombs in a repetitive almost identical manner. The most conflict we sense here is a brief cut to a baby crying and a cut back to the blank expression of the face of the bomber. We know that there must be comprehension of the horror that is about to unfold and we know that they must do the equations to allow themselves to commit these acts but we barely see it, we barely understand what it is like, these empty characters blow up more empty rag-doll nothings with French faces. It is beyond poor. It is ineffective, it feels pointless. Why make this film in the way it was made? What is being said here I can’t understand it? Is it really just to say the obvious? That the Algerians had courage and that the French were ignorant to the point of cruelty? We know this already, we are not stupid. I am drawing a blank. The filmmaking is also not very effective. I’ve already mentioned the poor structuring of the thing, scenes are repetitive and dull and without real tension, shots are sometimes well composed but mostly feel incidental as if entirely unplanned and it was just where the camera operator happened to be standing during that particular take. Cuts and transitions are clumsy, sometimes overly quick and passive. The music by Morricone is just fine and the mix is pretty terrible, ADR is done so lazily that almost no dialogue matches at all. At the end of the day it is fine but I’m always bewildered to find something like this sitting with such high regard. I feel insane. Ok that’s all 5/10.

While this film may seem like an almost shattering statement meant to invoke a sense of injustice within you as it details the wrongdoings of the government and the dangers of colonization, for me, it just seemed like pro-revolutionary propaganda, which, while that is a movement I completely think is justified, propaganda tends not to have much of anything beyond its purpose of making you say that's bad and that's good. I would've preferred a more introspective look into the lack of morality that revolution warrants in order to work, and the sacrifices that need to be made in order to continue it. This highlights, particularly, the oppression, racism, and the cruel generalization of the Arabs due to them only demanding that they want their home given back to them. It's reminiscent of Palestine's genocide, just on a smaller scale. The Battle of Algiers may be more of an exposition of what occurred in Algiers, with the intent of making the revolutionaries seem like heroes and the army look like an empire, which is why it is nowhere near my favorite film. Much like the many flaws OBAA had regarding its lack of any actual reflection or any sense of more abstract themes for me, both are still great films that only suffer from what they're missing. The film seeks to document the actions and the wrongdoings of the rebels and the army. It's not really followed by a plot, but rather an escalation of means as the rebels begin attaining more and more authority over the people of Algiers, and as they become a more prominent, symbolic force of hope for the people. What I did find more interesting was the French civilians' response to the rebels' attacks. The generalization and the prominent racism committed by them, while an understandable response to the rebels' terrorist attacks, is in no way excusable, and it's a concept I would've preferred to have seen more insight into. The army begins to employ "interrogation tactics" that in reality, are just glorified torture, and due to these, the entire rebel group begins to lose men. The film ends with them being wiped out from the map with the death of what I would say is the protagonist of the film. The best part for me was the ending, which was the insurrection of the Arabs against colonization by the French, and how the revolution serves as a catapult for them to join their efforts and unite. No longer were they going to be saved by a group of heroes; rather, they must be the heroes themselves. The film's themes are kind of empty. It's more about what the film shows you rather than what it indicates, which is my main issue with it. I hoped for some deeper statement on how revolution needs to be carried out with the disregard and the savagery that the oppressors have always fought with, and how that means that instead of being heroes or rebels in the most indicative sense, it would be redundant, and instead you must become something far darker, something far more immoral and soulless. You must echo the same brutality shown to you by the enemy so that you may prevail for your cause. Your intention may be different, but the consequences of your actions will be the same. Death in the name of a symbol; just that one is more hopeful and useful than the one employed by the opposition. This was nowhere to be found in the film, and while I understand that this film serves more as a documentation or a version of the story meant to entertain us, well, it lacking this kind of reflection really did a number on me because I like to think about films after watching them, and I felt almost nothing concerning this film's final statement. This is just personal preference, I suppose, and it has to do with the fact that I personally have more emotional connection to abstract themes rather than to evocative statements, so I guess you could say this just wasn't for me. The film's production was kind of insane now that I think about it? There are some explosions that really kind of surprised me due to the sheer impact of their force, and it makes me wonder if they actually did blow up buildings with people inside them. Anyways, the cinematography and the visuals obviously take a step back, considering this is a film that is heavily focused on telling its plot rather than being a good film. I think it's interesting how some parts were filmed, but in the visual department, I didn't find anything that really blew me away. The acting was also kind of disconnected from me because I think that the characters felt incredibly 1-dimensional and taken aback. It's more of a story in which the ideologies are the protagonists and the actual characters are just plot devices, which is not something I'm particularly fond of. The pacing was also incredibly long, and the entertainment value was just something that I didn't find, since it's a film that is stripped of any actual cinematic qualities. I'd like to say that it is an absolutely iconic reminder of the time and that its importance does not falter, but that also does not negate its qualities, which I didn't necessarily prefer.

The premise described on letterboxed doesn’t start until nearly 50 minutes in. Prior to that, all we’re watching are radical extremists blowing up random civilians, which eventually comes together into some measure of purpose by the end. The sparse but thoughtful lines of dialogue illuminate the different narratives we use to try to justify our actions. The torture, tricks, and escalating tactics can be effective at times, but the film is ultimately at odds with itself. It wants to depict the mechanizations of revolution without sympathetic characters, only sympathetic factions. That’s admirable, but then it relies on excessive crash zooms and close ups on random crying people, a cheap, easy way to get the viewer enraged. Though I shouldn’t say random because they’re almost always the radicals, who by the end, are just terrorists gunning down pedestrian women. The film is not as impartial as it wants us to think it is, and unfortunately, I found myself kinda siding with the colonists who by and large followed some kind of ethical code (even if random grunts broke it on occasion). The radicals, by contrast, were so conniving that it really did feel like the colonists had every right to be suspicious of them. I think we’re naturally drawn to side with the underdogs because we know that their options are far more limiting, but I also think if they’d focused on actually targeting the French military, instead of regular people, or otherwise did anything that showed them rustling with the moral lows they were stooping to, it would have revealed their humanity in a way that shoving a camera into someone’s face doesn’t.

La bataille d'Alger est un film incontournable sur la guerre d'Algérie, il est même le plus connu internationalement. Le film se déroule durant une période précise de la guerre que l'on appelle « la bataille d'Alger », période qui a duré de 1956 à 1957. Durant cette période, Alger devint un véritable champ de bataille où le FLN et l'armée française se sont livrés à des combats sans merci. Les deux camps ont fait preuve d'une extrême violence, notamment lors des attentats commis par le FLN contre des innocents ou encore à travers les tortures pratiquées par l'armée française. Cette violence, que l'on ressent tout au long du film, est caractéristique des régimes coloniaux, mais surtout des débuts de révolutions. En effet, Frantz Fanon , dans Les Damnés de la Terre , explique que la violence est une étape nécessaire pour que le colonisé, privé de toute initiative et de libertés intérieures et extérieures, retrouve ses droits. La violence extrême est donc nécessaire, mais elle constitue seulement la première étape de la révolution, elle n'est pas la révolution en soi. Cette étape de la révolte et de la lutte armée est la forme infantile de la révolution, c'est-à-dire qu'elle constitue le premier mouvement nécessaire, mais qu'ensuite tout le travail reste à faire. La révolte permet d'arriver à l'indépendance dans le cas de l'Algérie, qui devient officiellement indépendante le 5 juillet 1962. Ce mouvement d'insurrection fut impossible à canaliser pour l'armée française, malgré sa supériorité militaire, c'est pourquoi De Gaulle conclut progressivement qu'une Algérie française n'était pas durable. C'est donc par la violence et le courage que l'Algérie devint indépendante. Comme le souligne Fanon , le plus dur dans la révolution est l'après-révolte : une fois que les opprimés ont gagné, que faut-il faire ? Comment s'organiser ? En Algérie, Ben Bella fut le premier président en 1963, mais il fut renversé en 1965 par un coup d'État. C'est ensuite Boumédiène qui prit la relève en renforçant le poids de l'État dans l'économie. Des politiques d'industrialisation (Industries industrialisantes ou modèle Feldman-Mahalanobis) furent mises en œuvre, mais avec un succès limité, car cette stratégie d'industrialisation est autocentrée et nécessite donc une forte demande intérieure. Or, en Algérie, la population représentait alors moins de 40 millions d'habitants. Cependant, grâce au pétrole et au gaz (95 % des recettes d'exportation algériennes), l'État a pu financer certains projets tout en restant fermé au tourisme et à une grande partie du commerce extérieur. Aujourd'hui, les relations franco-algériennes sont tendues. L'affaire Boualem Sansal en est un exemple. Il existe toujours des frictions entre les deux États, notamment autour du Sahara occidental et du passé colonial français.

Watching Black & White Movies #5 Twentieth-century evil for me is embodied in the terrorization of militaries operating brutally, efficiently, and without remorse. Yes, Mathieu embodies this threat. But don’t Ali La Pointe and Saadi Yacef Djafar as well? In that sense, the film is careful to show that history’s judgment depends on which side of it you occupy (eg. maybe French colonialism is bad and the french suck!) What the film captures exceptionally well is the terror created by war, portraying both sides in meticulous detail. The reason I rated it so low is that this documentary-style approach leaves Mathieu as the only substantially developed character. As a result, I find it difficult to see the film as a full exploration of its subject; it’s a documentary-esque sequence of events, but not a “complete” examination of the conflict. Its nuance is incomplete. Rather than offering a truly comprehensive portrayal, it presents a focused account that inevitably privileges certain perspectives over others. Un excellent film où le cinéma d’action moderne est né. Un film politique du réalisateur italien Gillo Pontecorvo. La manière dont le film est produit est juste glaçante, même radicale. Basé sur la lutte pour l’indépendance algérienne, c’est un film qui brûle la rétine et le cœur du spectateur, assistant à cela jusqu’au point d’éveiller les consciences. Les acteurs sont bien choisis et ciblés de manière très précise. On ne cherche pas de grandes stars hollywoodiennes mais des visages de haine marqués par cet épisode colonial, qui retransmettent leur identité de combattant au téléspectateur. Les décors également, on veut de l’authenticité jusqu’au bout. On tourne dans la vraie Casbah d’Alger où, quelques années auparavant, des guérillas avaient véritablement eu lieu. Les plans également sont aussi un chef-d’œuvre. La caméra, tenue par Marcello Mastroianni, jette toutes les règles et tous les codes du monde du cinéma, filmant à portée de main pour nous introduire dans le monde réel qu’a vécu l’Algérie durant cette conquête coloniale. Il filme comme on court dans la Casbah, comment on se cache, comment on respire ainsi que l’on combat. Des cadres parfois instables, flous, mais totalement choisis pour l’immersion la plus totale, avec un vrai style tremblant de réalité. En conclusion, un film d’une expérience hors norme, nous faisant vibrer tout au long du visionnage, en comprenant la vie des algériens durant 132 ans de conquête coloniale sanglante menée par la France.

What a setting to watch this film for the first time. The AFI Fellows audience was deathly silent throughout the whole screening. There is so little levity of any kind to hold onto. Every time I felt I could justify one side's view, the film deliberately introduced a more complex perspective, forcing me to reconsider. I think THE BATTLE OF ALGIERS represents a small miracle. As powerful as the story is, I am more inspired and impressed that this story was allowed to be told in the first place. In the end, I especially related to the occupied citizens of Algiers, especially those who sacrificed everything for the cause of freedom. When it comes to war, there are no winners. My fundamental belief is that when we turn to violence, the consequences are far too many and complex to understand, let alone decide a victor. But the Algerian people deserved their freedom, and witnessing their drive for that cause lights a fire in me. This is what great movies do! I hope to use this battle cry in my own ventures into storytelling.

The film *The Battle of Algiers* depicts the era of the French occupation of Algeria, a time when Algerian resistance fighters battled the French army in pursuit of independence and freedom. Central to this struggle was the National Liberation Front (FLN), which a young man named Ali La Pointe joined; the Front’s goal was to defeat the French and secure liberty. Although the French army—led by Colonel Mathieu—ultimately dismantled the Front, resulting in the deaths of Ali and his comrades, the Algerians did not surrender. They eventually won their independence in 1962, ending more than 140 years of French occupation and humiliation. This history demonstrates the patience and courage of the Algerian people—from the youngest child to the oldest elder—who truly achieved independence and freedom after enduring immense suffering It is an absolutely magnificent film—one of the greatest historical war movies—depicting the period in Algeria just a few years prior to independence. It was presented in a style akin to a documentary, yet it was truly outstanding. A lot of my favorite movies, their very existence is a miracle. ‘The Battle Of Algiers’ is no exception, with both the uphill backstory of the FLN driving France out of their country and, as people with no experience in film making, producing a movie about this series of historical events. “Can you separate the art from the artist?” okay sure but can you separate the art from history? Before getting into that, in a vacuum this is a thrilling movie that succeeds in filling its viewer with on-the-edge-of-their seat uncertainty of what’s to come. Just like when one watches ‘Titanic’ we know how it ends but we still get wrapped up in what’s happening. It would be impossible to spoil ‘The Battle Of Algiers’, no series of words can summarize the experience of watching, feeling. The sequence leading up to the first explosions in civilian areas goes toe to toe with the most well made suspense/thrillers. Of which, one of the biggest strengths of ‘The Battle Of Algiers’ is how it portrays its subjects. Obviously we are meant to empathize with the FLN fighters, but it doesn’t stop there. The “bad guys”, the French, aren’t shown in a two dimensional villainous manner. (which is in stark contrast to the recently released ‘I Am Cuba’, two years prior.) Even the main antagonist Colonel Phillippe Mathieu is shown as intelligent, cunning, capable. Maybe emphathize is the wrong word, “humanize” might be better. But what are we supposed to think when there’s emphasis on a baby licking an ice cream cone moments before the explosion that will brutally maim, kill them? In the same breath, we see the uncertainty (?) of the women before erupting carnage. There is a depth here that is absent in nearly all movies built around these types of events. Especially made in the U.S. where all terrorists are painted with evil brushes. No matter where you lie politically, ‘The Battle Of Algiers’ is a must watch that will either add to your perspective or straight up twist it into something different. I can see why the Black Panthers used to screen this for each other. (Or why it was included in ‘One Battle After Another’ as a way for Leonardo Di Caprio’s character to relive his days of fighting the forces at large.) This rewatch has cemented the film in my Top 10 Of All Time. It is a miracle of film making no doubt.

La Batalla de Argel afronta esa pregunta con una madurez infinitamente mayor, sin medias tintas, sin buenos y malos. Nos explica cómo la complejidad de las circunstancias pueden llevar a que el “no matarás” no parezca más que una formalidad. TOP 28 LETTERBOXD! FULL REVIEW! Where other war movies fall short at showing the full brutality of war, this shows it in the most extraordinary way, unlike anything you'll ever see. Gripping, intense, and suspenseful; it feels so realistic that you'll be tricked into thinking that some of these scenes come from found footage. In The Battle of Algiers , they show that during wartime, humans forfeit their morals and jurisdiction to achieve their goals by doing whatever it takes. But they show it from both sides: the Algerian rebellion and the French government. What’s even more interesting is that the Algerians are played by actual Algerians, all non-professional actors, some of whom had actually fought for the FLN. They show the injustice and oppression the French brought upon them. French law enforcement murder innocent people and use bombs, to the point where the Algerians can’t let it pass anymore. So they use the same violence as a form of retaliation. We get a peek at how rebels actually fight against their oppressors, and we root for them because of it. There isn’t a main character, but that’s not even necessary because the message, story, and plot are what’s important. We see multiple characters who get their moments, and we actually care for them in such a short span of time. When they execute a plan, we’re glued to the screen because of the intensity. Ennio Morricone’s music sounds like a ticking time bomb during those suspenseful moments. There is no melodrama: this is the real thing. What’s intriguing is that Algerians are depicted not as one-dimensional characters, but as the centre of the story. They terrorize, but we get to see their motivations beforehand: oppression, over a century of colonialism, and innocent people being murdered. French laws and repression created the conditions for the rebellion, and the Algerians give the French a taste of their own medicine, but the French come back even more fiercely. This is the story of what has been happening throughout history, and what is still happening today. That’s what makes this movie so timeless and important. Dangerous people grab power and start wars for their own personal gain, but lead their own people astray by distorting their viewpoint. Like Vladimir Putin, for example: a clever and dangerous man with an enormous amount of power, willing to go to war against Ukraine in pursuit of Russian power and influence, while justifying it through distorted arguments. Colonel Mathieu (Jean Martin) represents those dangerous men with enough power to break through all morals and laws. When we get introduced to Colonel Mathieu, we can already tell: this guy is bad news. This is a person who is dangerously clever and is there to stop the terrorists by whatever means necessary...
